title: The death penalty (CCC 2267)
hook: the Catechism's paragraph 2267 was rewritten to call the death penalty inadmissible

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gospel of life: life more abundantly, and a wide list of threats to it. Your line was every life counts. Who did you check in on? Day one thousand three hundred eleven.

A few verses after Abel's death in Genesis, Cain, the killer, is afraid: whoever finds him, he says, will kill him. And then something unexpected. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord set a mark upon Cain, that whosoever found him should not kill him." The killer walks away guilty, sent out, and protected. That small mark sits behind a paragraph in the Catechism of the Catholic Church, number 2267, which Pope Francis approved in new words. Today's word is its subject: the death penalty.
screen: `CAIN IS AFRAID.` → `A MARK, SO NO ONE KILLS HIM.` → `PARAGRAPH 2267.`

segments.voice: First, the older wording. The Catechism used to say that the Church's traditional teaching did not rule out the death penalty, if it was the only way to protect people's lives from an unjust aggressor. It added, drawing on John Paul the Second's gospel of life, that cases where that is truly necessary are very rare, if not practically nonexistent. A door left open, but only a crack. Second, the new wording. The revised paragraph says that the death penalty is inadmissible, because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person, and that the Church works with determination for its abolition worldwide. Inadmissible: not allowed in, not something the Church can accept. Third, the reasons it gives. A growing awareness that a person's dignity is not lost, even after very serious crimes. A new understanding of what punishment by the state is for. And ways of detaining dangerous people that protect the public without closing off the guilty person's chance to change. John Paul the Second, in yesterday's letter, read Cain's mark the same way: not even a murderer loses his dignity. The Church presents the change as a development of its teaching in the light of the gospel, and Catholic writers have discussed how it fits with what came before. Fourth, the people involved. Jesus in Matthew names among the works that matter, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in prison, and you came to me." And the Church also keeps close the families of victims, whose grief is real and deserves care. Both are held in the same hands.
screen: `THE OLD WORDING: A DOOR LEFT AJAR.` · `THE NEW WORDING: INADMISSIBLE.` · `DIGNITY ISN'T LOST, EVEN AFTER CRIME.` · then, large: `I WAS IN PRISON, AND YOU CAME TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for prisoners on death row. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a prison cell you've never seen: a narrow bed, a small window or none, a person waiting. You don't need to know their crime or decide anything about it. Just let them be a person. Then widen the circle: the guards who work there, the chaplain who visits, the families of the people who were harmed, still grieving. Give each one a breath. If you pray, you can hold them all before God together. If you don't, hold them in mind without sorting them. The bell holds the time.
The death penalty. Which the Catechism now calls inadmissible, an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person, even a guilty one. Today's word.

Your line: inadmissible. Today, when you hear someone written off as beyond saving, in the news or in conversation, remember Cain's mark, and hold back the final word. Day one thousand three hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Catholics act on this teaching through prison ministry, visits and letters to people on death row, support for victims' families, and advocacy for the abolition of the death penalty, and bishops' conferences in several countries speak publicly on it.

fork.setup: a man has done something terrible. he is locked away and the public is safe. what does the revised Catechism say about putting him to death?
options: it's allowed whenever a court decides.
it's inadmissible: his dignity is not lost.
fork.reveal: paragraph 2267 now calls the death penalty inadmissible, an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person, and the Church works for its abolition.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Church has always simply been for, or against, the death penalty.
what it means: the Catechism now calls it inadmissible, because a guilty person keeps their dignity.
what a scholar hears: CCC 2267 revised, building on Evangelium Vitae 56, and presented as a development of doctrine.

notes: The index hook says 'in 2018'; the voice gives no year (the claims rule: the cited Catechism text does not state the date). The 'hook' field here is reworded to avoid the date; the index hook is unchanged.

Both the earlier and revised texts of CCC 2267 are paraphrased; key phrases ('inadmissible', 'inviolability and dignity of the person', 'abolition worldwide', 'very rare, if not practically non-existent') are used unquoted. Confirm.
The three reasons are paraphrased from the revised CCC 2267; confirm.

'Presented as a development' rests on the CDF letter to bishops accompanying the revision; 'Catholic writers have discussed how it fits' is a soft, fair description of the debate. A Keeper may wish to adjust.
'The first murderer in the Bible' is drawn from Genesis 4 itself (Cain's is the first killing the Bible narrates). Cut if read as a superlative claim.
